# pokefit

> pokefit (https://pokefit.party) is a free web tool that scales a 3D-printable figure (3MF, STL, OBJ or GLB) to the
> largest size that fits inside a printed Pokéball, cuts 1–3 magnet pockets into its underside so it snaps onto
> a thin steel disc (or a washer) glued inside the ball, checks printability, and exports a Bambu Studio-ready 3MF that keeps
> painted colours. It runs entirely in the browser (Python compiled to WebAssembly via Pyodide); files are not
> uploaded. A local Python version adds Bambu Studio slicing for print time and filament use.

## What it does

- Fit: largest scale at which the figure fits the ball's inner sphere, the connector rings near the equator and
  the ring opening it must pass through when the ball closes, with a chosen clearance (default 1 mm). The figure
  stands on the steel, glued on a flat floor filled into the bottom of the ball. The floor's diameter is chosen per
  figure (the one that lets it fit largest: a wider floor sits higher, where the sphere is wider, so a wide figure
  fits much larger on a thin disc; a tall narrow one keeps the low floor), or typed (a shell already printed); the
  exported bottom shell is cut to match.
- Ball size: the 60 % or 100 % print of the MakerWorld model "functional Pokéball – no glue" (#2045372), or any
  inner diameter in millimetres (the ring profile scales with it).
- Magnets: 1, 2 or 3 pockets (default Ø4.18 × 2.2 mm, for 4 × 2 mm disc magnets) placed automatically to spread
  out over the steel (anywhere on a solid disc, its middle too; on a washer's ring, not over its hole); draggable
  by hand. By default every pocket opens on the steel, so the magnet
  touches the steel; under a part that floats above the bed the magnet shows below it (at least 0.5 mm of the
  pocket must be in the figure). A "raised" option moves pockets up into such parts instead (hidden magnet, weaker
  hold), up to 2 mm above the steel. Nothing goes below the plane the figure stands on.
- Shape for the ball (on by default): the ball's floor is flat only over the printed floor; beyond it the
  sphere rises. Legs or a tail lying flat out past it are lifted along the sphere's curve (eased in, the
  lowest 30 % of the figure's height lifted fully, fading above, so arms and head are untouched). Automatic
  strength comes from the share of the low footprint beyond the steel disc that is a limb (free space above it, not a
  solid column) and the low footprint's aspect ratio; it is kept only if the figure then fits ≥ 1 % larger. The
  base over the steel disc is made flat: bumps pressed down by up to 1.2 mm, then gaps up to 2.5 mm between the
  underside and the floor (the figure's lowest point) filled by a separate solid "flat base" part, never taller than
  the gap it fills (plus 0.4 mm hidden inside the figure) (main colour; at the default, raised to 4
  or 6 mm when the magnets asked for do not fit otherwise, e.g. a figure on four thin legs). Air above a low piece is
  a gap too: a paw on the bed under a leg starting within the fill height is filled up to the leg, so pockets beside
  it are walled; when fewer magnets fit than asked, the Magnets card offers the deeper fill. "Fill where": round the steel disc
  (joined to where the figure stands), everywhere under the figure (every part hovering up to the fill height is
  filled down to the bed), inside a circle the user places and drags, or inside an outline the user draws in the
  underside view. With the magnets on the steel, each pocket also gets a pad of the same fill (gaps up to the
  fill height under its walled disc), so the magnet is walled from the steel up; pocket placement counts on
  the pads. Only
  vertices move, so paint and texture colour are kept. Settings: bend Auto/Off/Slight/Medium/Follow the sphere,
  flat base diameter (default the steel disc's), press depth, fill height, fill where.
- Reshape a part: "Pick a part", tap a tail, ear, leg or arm (found up to the valley where it meets the body, like
  paint's Part mode; a joint-angle slider moves where it ends), then Size (30-300 %), Bend (tip up or down; a part
  pointing up or down tips to the front or back) and Swing (sideways), about the joint. The change eases in over the
  first third of the part (walking along its surface), so it bends in a curve and the body is untouched; only
  vertices move, so paint is kept. The fit, floor and magnets follow the new shape. Nothing stops a part bent into
  the body. Base width (x1-x3), Reach (5-100 % of the part's length) and Taper (0.25-4): strengthen where it joins by
  widening only the part's base about its own centre line, fading to nothing at the reach (taper below 1 stays wide
  for longer, above 1 falls off right after the joint); the rest of the part keeps its size.
- Strengthen thin parts (off by default; 1.2 / 1.6 / 2 mm): local thickness is measured at the print size (voxels
  and a distance transform); only across a feature (where the inward ray leaves the solid within ~1.5-3 x its
  thickness), so points and rims (ear tips, a lightning-bolt tail's point) keep their shape instead of swelling into
  knobs; a thin feature (ear, tail tip, flame) gets the minimum where it joins the figure,
  tapering to 40 % of it at its tip, and a thin neck between two thick parts gets it all along. The thickening is
  built as a solid (an offset of the surface on a 0.1 mm grid, smoothed, united with the figure), blended into the
  surface around and never more than about half way into a gap: fine relief under it (an ear's incised line and
  panel) fills smoothly instead of crumpling. Colours carry onto it from the nearest painted triangle; taps and
  paint still name the figure's own triangles. It can take tens of seconds on a spiky 300k-triangle figure (about a
  minute in the browser engine; "Thickening thin parts…" shows meanwhile). It is per figure, not remembered.
- Weak points (Figure card, "Find weak points"): every thin part (thinner than 3 mm at the print size: an ear, a tail,
  a claw) is graded by the push at its far end that would snap it at its weakest section (bending: strength x section
  modulus / lever; about half the strength where the section lies flat, so the layers pull apart). A holds ~2 kg, B
  ~800 g, C ~300 g, D ~100 g, F less or under 0.8 mm across. A cantilever rod 1.5 mm x 10 mm measures 1.34 N against
  1.33 N by the beam formula. Each can be shown on the view and thickened on its own ("Thicken", per-feature
  strengthen: only that part, from its weak section to where it already holds grade C). It is stretched across its
  thin direction (vertices move, no triangles are added): veins, outline and paint stay, and it tapers towards the tip
  as the load does. A 300k figure takes ~12 s to grade and ~30 s to thicken on a PC, ~18 s and ~40 s in the browser
  engine. "Print weak parts solid" instead adds Bambu modifier volumes over grade C-F
  parts in the export (6 walls, 100 % infill): the shape stays; nothing changes when the process already prints 100 %
  infill (Bambu's X2D 0.20 mm Standard does).
- Changes to your model (top of the Figure card): every setting reshaping the figure now (simplified, parts reshaped,
  legs bent, base pressed or filled, thickened), where it came from (your last figure, the default, set now) and an
  Undo; its control is marked. A setting carried over from the last figure that reshapes the new one is also announced
  as the file opens.
- Height: a height in mm can be set (also before opening a file); it is used unless it does not fit, then the
  largest that fits is used, with a note. Settings that are changed (ball, steel, floor, magnets, pockets, height, shape,
  simplify, paint depth, specks) are remembered in the browser as the defaults; "reset settings" in the
  footer clears them. Settings set before a file is opened are used for its first analysis.
- Simplify mesh: a dense mesh (sculpts and scans of hundreds of thousands to millions of triangles) is cut when it
  loads, like Bambu Studio's Simplify: levels Low / Medium / High keep 7 / 20 / 50 % of the file's triangles (the
  setting is a share, so a level means the same on every file), a log-scale slider picks any share from 1 % up,
  and any triangle count can be typed (from 1,000). A figure of more than 300,000 triangles opens simplified to
  200,000 unless Simplify was set (or that option is unticked), or it is a pokefit export (opened as made: its
  paint is not resampled); Off keeps every triangle. Quadric edge collapse with even
  triangle sizes (meshoptimizer's own WebAssembly build, the same in the browser and the local version), never
  moving the surface by more than 0.1 % of the figure's size. A glTF's colours are sampled on the new triangles;
  a painted 3MF keeps one colour per triangle. Measured on a 1.45M-triangle Eevee at 100k: open 39.5 -> 11.5 s,
  a paint tap 0.8 -> 0.03 s, export 13.5 -> 1.4 s, surface change 0.017 mm at 25 mm tall.
- Mesh repair (like Bambu Studio's "Fix model", automatic): when a file loads, and after every boolean (magnet
  pockets, overlapping parts, the flat base), every part is made so each edge joins exactly two triangles, also
  after welding vertices by position (Bambu Studio's "non-manifold edges" check): vertices welded, degenerate and
  folded triangles dropped, edges shared by more than two triangles separated into pairs (by angle about the edge,
  each pair enclosing solid), stray extra triangles dropped, neighbours turned to agree and inside-out shells
  turned, holes closed by fans, and points where separate surfaces touch moved apart by 0.001 mm. The analysis
  says what loading repaired ("Mesh repaired"). Paint and a glTF's colours follow their triangles.
- GLB / glTF (single file): every mesh node is baked in and Y-up metres become Z-up mm (a scene over 10 units is
  kept as mm). Its colour (a texture, including the emissive slot some AI generators use; vertex colours; or flat
  materials) is sampled on sub-triangles laid out as Bambu's paint brush splits them, clustered into a few filament
  colours (shading ignored, a chosen 1–16, or automatic: the best-value count, the one before an added colour
  would cost many more filament changes, else as many as the file clearly has, up to 8; never more than 2 h of
  colour changes), cleared of specks, and
  written as split Bambu paint on one solid part, so it slices multi-colour with crisp edges. Fewer filaments =
  less purge waste and print time; each palette size's estimated cost is shown. "Keep details" (+1 to +3
  filaments) keeps small features that contrast most with the colour they would merge into (black pupils on a
  cream head) as their own filaments: on two Squirtle models, 2 colours + 1 detail kept the pupils for +49 to
  +73 min in Bambu slices, against 4-5 colours otherwise.
- Colorize: paint single-colour models by tapping the 3D view (while painting, the palette, modes and tools sit on the
  3D view itself; foldable). A tap fills a part found from the geometry (spread
  until a concave valley sharper than an angle, default 15°, where ears, tails, legs or eyes meet the body), any
  crease (like Bambu's smart fill), a separate shell, or a brush disc; dragging the brush paints a stroke, and a
  part or crease fill stops where the colour changes (outline an eye or a belly that has no crease round it, then
  tap inside), or "Fill" (a bucket fill that crosses every crease and stops only where the colour changes).
  The default "Wand" (magic wand) takes the feature tapped - an eye, a flame, a toe pad - from the shape alone: closed
  loops round the tap that follow the surface's bends, and limb-like regions, scored by how strong their edge is all
  the way round; Smaller / Larger step through the other sizes it found. It needs the feature in the geometry (a
  decimated mesh whose eyes were flattened away has nothing to find). "Prints from" lists every palette colour,
  including ones not painted yet. "Thicken thin parts to" goes up to 4 mm; the underside view shows the gap fill
  (flat base) in its own colour.
  Soft edges: the wand, brush and stamp (and any step grown or shrunk) paint with a smooth edge cut through the
  triangles, written as split Bambu paint, so an eye is an oval and not a stepped outline; a later fill bounded
  by colour fills up to that edge, inside split triangles too. "Stamp": drag a box over a spot and the ellipse
  in it is painted like a decal on the surfaces facing the view (for eyes a decimated mesh no longer outlines).
  "Shape map": the figure shaded by its creases (dark) and relief (warm raised, cool sunk) with contour lines of
  equal relief, drawn per vertex: the structure the wand follows. Grow / Shrink are exact to a few per cent.
  Mirror paints the same spot on the other side too (the figure's mirror plane, found from its shape; asymmetric
  spots such as a curled tail paint one side). Grow / Shrink widen or narrow the last step along the surface in
  0.1 mm steps; Cover line (L) paints the last wand/part/crease/fill step over the engraved line round it too, so
  an eye or panel cut out by a groove is not left with a ring of the body colour: the engine measures the groove's
  width along the outline (depth under a grey closing of the surface's relief, smallest closing scale where the
  line is full depth) and widens the step to its far rim with a smooth edge; Pick colour selects the colour under a tap; Undo / Redo; keyboard shortcuts on desktop. "Drop
  specks under" (default 0.5 mm²) gives tiny painted patches the colour around them, since each would cost a
  filament change on every layer it spans; a patch that is most of one paint step (an eye's small oval tapped on
  purpose) is kept: only what a step leaves of another, and the file's own stray specks, go. "Split by piece" gives each separate patch of the selected colour its own
  filament (white eyes and a white tail: three colours); the largest keeps the colour, patches under 0.5 mm² (or the
  speck size) stay, new filaments take the colour most unlike the palette, and Undo takes it back in one step.
  "Colours from a picture" (Colours card): official art by Pokémon name or national number (the name is suggested
  from the file and figure names, typos allowed; artwork from PokeAPI's sprites repository) or any picture opened,
  dropped on the page or pasted; tap the picture or one of its main colours (k-means in CIELAB, each named by its
  most common exact colour) to set the selected filament, or "Match the palette": each filament takes the most
  common exact colour among the picture's pixels within 15 ΔE of its closest one (none within 45: kept); Undo match.
  "Remove colour" deletes the selected colour from the palette: the file's own colour and paint steps in it take the
  closest remaining colour (CIE76) and later filaments move down one (Params.colour_map renumbers the file's
  filaments before paint steps); Undo restores it.
- Re-opening an export: pokefit's own pockets are found from their shape (a flat round ceiling over vertical walls
  facing its axis all round, joined across parts), filled in, and the magnets placed there again as pockets placed by
  hand; the export's "flat base" parts are dropped (made again from the settings: an export records the base settings
  it was made with in Metadata/pokefit.json, flat base / depth / gap fill / fill area, and opens with them, so a figure
  exported without a press or gap fill does not gain one; not remembered for the next figure). Both are applied
  before the first analysis, so an export opens in one pass. Checked on 7 round trips (found
  within 0.001 mm) and 5 original figures (none found). Painting prepares the figure's regions when it starts. Colours can be added or changed; the result
  is written as Bambu per-triangle paint (paint_color), so it slices as multi-colour. "Prints from" shows each
  figure colour's slot (the user's project slots, or the printer's AMS trays locally) in a dropdown with colour
  swatches, closest colour first with its ΔE (with the AMS read: which nozzle each spool feeds, and "No spool"
  when nothing loaded is close); the palette swatches carry the slot they print from. "Paint depth"
  sets how far colours reach into the figure (Bambu's segmented-region width; inside is the main filament): it
  changes how much of each colour is used, not the print time or the colour changes.
- Export: the Bambu 3MF (and its import variant), the bottom shell STL with the floor for the steel, a JSON report, and a coloured STL: the
  figure and its flat base joined into one closed solid (every edge on two triangles, vertices matched exactly),
  soft paint edges written as their sub-triangles, each triangle's colour in the STL attribute word (VisCAM /
  SolidView: bit 15 set, 5 bits each of red, green, blue). MeshLab, VisCAM and SolidView show the colours; Bambu
  Studio and most slicers load the shape only.
- Steel: thin steel discs (20.3 × 0.25 mm = 0.8" × 0.01", the default, and 15 × 0.5 mm = 0.59" × 0.02") and
  washers (DIN 9021 M5/M6/M8, US #10 × 3/4", US 1/4" × 1" fender), or a custom size (hole 0 = a disc); a comparison
  table shows the largest figure each allows on this figure's floor with the magnets on steel. Stainless steel is
  not magnetic.
- View: Ball off shows the figure alone (no shell, ring, steel or floor); Cut halves the ball; Space shows the usable
  space.
- Orientation: rotate about X, Y and Z by any angle; the lowest point lands on the bed.
- Checks: closed surface, normals, degenerate faces, separate shells, wall thickness (warn < 0.8 mm, fail when
  more than 5 % is < 0.4 mm), overhangs flatter than the slicer's support angle, layers that start in mid-air,
  bed contact (brim advice), and per pocket: wall, ceiling, height above the steel, position over the steel.
- Export: the figure as a Bambu Studio 3MF (opens as a project, painted colours kept); an "import" variant whose
  filament numbers are matched by colour to the user's own Bambu project slots (for File > Import > Import
  geometry only); a JSON report; and, if the user loads their copy of the ball model, the bottom shell with the flat
  floor for the steel filled in. (Bambu Studio 2.8.2 says "invalid config, load geometry data only" on every
  geometry-only import of any 3MF: it skips the file's settings and its check fails on the empty ones; fixed in
  2.9.1.)
- Bambu presets: besides a project 3MF, the settings button reads Bambu Studio's preset exports (File > Export >
  Export Preset Bundle: a .bbscfg printer bundle, a .bbsflmt filament bundle, or a printer/filament/process
  presets .zip). A preset is a diff over a system preset (`inherits`); the local version resolves it against the
  installed Bambu Studio's profiles, the browser lays it over the project's closest slot (marked approximate).
  Filament presets become selectable materials, process presets for the same printer a "Process" choice, a
  printer preset for the project's printer is applied, and a filament whose temperature for the project's plate
  is 0 is flagged (Bambu refuses to slice it).
- Colour-change cost: per layer, which filaments print (from the paint); per nozzle, the changes when it
  keeps its loaded filament; on a two-nozzle printer (X2D, H2D) the best split of filaments between nozzles.
  Shown as filament changes, extra time and purge grams, for the figure and for every palette size of a
  textured GLB. Calibrated on Bambu CLI slices (about 105 s and 0.4 g per change, 18 s per nozzle switch);
  exports keep Bambu's own "Auto For Flush" nozzle assignment, which matched or beat the planner.
- Handoff from other apps: `?url=<model URL>` (CORS), or open pokefit and post
  `{type: "pokefit:load", name, data: ArrayBuffer}` after it announces `pokefit:ready` (trusted origins only).
- Multi-figure 3MF files: a picker chooses which figure to fit.

## Local version

- Source: https://github.com/tribixbite/pokefit (Python 3.11+, numpy/scipy/trimesh/manifold3d/shapely; web UI in
  TypeScript with three.js, built with bun).
- `pip install -e .`, then `python -m pokefit serve --open` (web UI with Bambu Studio slicing: 1× and 10× plate
  print time, filament grams, supports verdict) or `python -m pokefit fit figure.3mf --diameter 44 --magnets 2
  --out DIR --slice`.

## Notes

- Licence: GNU AGPL v3.0 or later (source: https://github.com/tribixbite/pokefit).
- Local version with beambam: reads the printer's AMS spools and matches the figure's colours to them; the
  Printer card shows the printer's live camera and progress (read-only). "Send to printer" on a sliced file shows
  which spool feeds each filament plus beambam's check of the G-code (time, grams, tool changes, purge, nozzle
  swaps, warnings; it reads the file only) before an explicit "Start print".
- Not affiliated with Nintendo, Game Freak, Creatures or The Pokémon Company.
- Contact / issues: https://github.com/tribixbite/pokefit/issues
